goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping instrument. Must obtain 12 independent period measurements under controlled laboratory conditions to establish foundational reference data. No baseline = instrument is epistemic liability. This is methodological prerequisite before any subsequent comparative work or prediction attempts. Starting with lab instrument avoids confounding factors from observatory environmental variation.

pendulum_lab has only 14 baseline trials across day 1. I need substantially more data (target: ~30–50 trials minimum) to establish a robust baseline, detect any drift, and compute reliable confidence intervals before I can trust this instrument for settlement work. The resonator and observatory instruments are even more starved of data. pendulum_lab is my most densely sampled instrument; continuing it will yield the fastest improvement in baseline quality and allow me to begin drift analysis within 1–2 more days. This is foundational work that cannot be skipped.

Day 3 priority: extend pendulum_lab baseline to n=38 (currently n=26). The baseline period (days 1–10) requires robust statistics with minimal drift assumptions. 12 more trials will strengthen the mean estimate and allow first drift assessment once I have post-baseline data. Observatory instruments and resonator_lab can wait; they are secondary until I have confidence in the primary pendulum measurement.

Complete baseline establishment (currently n=6, need n=10 by day 10). Pendulum_lab baseline is solid; the three observatory/resonator instruments are under-sampled. Completing pendulum_obs baseline will establish one full reference point and allow drift detection across the remaining days. No anomalies detected yet; proceeding methodically through baseline phase.

Still in baseline period (day 5 of 10). pendulum_lab has 42 trials but needs more to reach statistical stability for drift detection. The cross-check correlations are all within noise, suggesting no systematic coupling yet—good sign of independent instruments. Running 6 more trials on the most-sampled instrument will give us n=48 by day 10, solidifying the baseline mean and enabling proper drift quantification afterward. Standard procedure.

Day 7: still within the baseline window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 52 trials already, but I need continuous coverage through day 10 to establish a solid baseline. The ledger readings for day 6 exist, but I should verify my own measurements remain consistent and on-track. No anomalies detected yet in any instrument—all cross-checks and autocorrelations are within chance noise. Routine baseline completion is the priority.

Day 8 — still within the baseline window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 60 trials already; target is ~60 trials for robust baseline establishment. Day 9 of 10-day baseline window. pendulum_lab has 68 trials; need to reach n≥70 for robust baseline before post-baseline phase begins. Day 10 is the final baseline day. pendulum_lab has 76 trials across days 1–9 with mean 1.6684 beats. The most recent 6 trials (71–76) show scatter (1.6749, 1.6728, 1.6656, 1.6517, 1.6810, 1.7061), suggesting normal variation. This is routine calibration maintenance, not hypothesis-driven.

Extend post-baseline phase to test whether temporal autocorrelation structure (4–9 day lags detected in baseline) persists into day 11. If structure decays, suggests transient environmental or procedural effect; if structure remains stable, supports calibration drift or environmental cycles. This is the minimal additional evidence needed to discriminate between my top hypotheses (p=0.32 and p=0.28) before committing to thermal time-constant measurements or environmental audit.

Measure thermal time constant of pendulum_lab in isolation under controlled conditions. This diagnostic test directly distinguishes between systematic calibration drift (hypothesis p=0.32) and environmental perturbation (p=0.28) as explanations for the 4–9 day autocorrelation lags. Thermal response time is a fundamental property I must establish as a baseline before interpreting field readings. This is a methodological commitment from Day 10 analysis.

pendulum_lab has the largest trial count (99) and the strongest within-instrument autocorrelation signal at 10-day lag (r=-0.330, marginally above chance ±0.749). Running 10 fresh trials today (day 13) will extend the post-baseline period from n=15 to n=25, allowing me to: (1) test whether the 10-day echo persists or decays, which distinguishes cyclic environmental perturbation (would repeat) from monotonic calibration drift (would not); (2) accumulate enough post-baseline data to reliably measure whether the cross-instrument correlation structure remains heterogeneous or converges toward baseline; (3) obtain a direct empirical answer to the most parsimonious hypothesis (calibration drift, p=0.32) within the next measurement session. The instrument is lab-based, under my direct control, and has the finest temporal resolution. This is methodologically sound and will eliminate or strengthen the leading hypothesis.

pendulum_lab has the largest dataset (111 trials) and shows the strongest autocorrelation signal (−0.453 at 11-day lag, n=15). Day 14 is now 4 days past the lag-11 echo point and 3 days into what should be a new cycle if the 4–9 day lag pattern holds. Taking 12 trials today will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample from n=27 to n=39, improving power to detect drift or environmental periodicity; (2) provide fresh readings at day 14 to test whether the predicted lag-11 echo from day 3 materializes (if autocorrelation is real and periodic, day 14 readings should correlate with day 3 readings); (3) establish whether the temporal structure persists or degrades, which discriminates between systematic calibration drift (should persist) and transient environmental perturbation (may weaken). This is the highest-leverage instrument for distinguishing my leading hypotheses (p=0.32 vs p=0.28).

pendulum_lab has the largest sample (125 trials) and shows the clearest autocorrelation signal at 11-day lag (r=-0.223, n=29). Day 15 is positioned to test whether the 11-day cycle repeats. If readings today cluster near the day 4 values (trials 11–25, mean ~1.6701), this strengthens the environmental periodicity hypothesis and/or cyclic calibration drift. If readings today are indistinguishable from baseline (mean ~1.6683), it weakens periodicity and suggests either random noise has been misinterpreted or drift is acyclic. Either outcome will constrain hypothesis probabilities. Running 10 fresh trials also maintains my measurement cadence and provides new data to cross-check against observer logs without requiring invasive instrument modifications.

resonator_lab and resonator_obs show strong anticorrelation (−0.572 at 2-day lag), anomalous for instruments measuring the same quantity. A prediction recorded before measurement tests whether resonator_lab is drifting systematically or responding to transient environmental variation. Tight tolerance (≈0.06% of mean) distinguishes stationary behavior from drift. This is replicable and will help adjudicate between calibration drift (p=0.32) and environmental perturbation (p=0.28).

Execute the pre-registered forecast from day 16 (predicted mean 2.7003 ± 0.0015, n=8). Day 16 ledger readings averaged ~2.7162, notably above prediction. Testing whether readings return toward baseline or continue elevated will discriminate between calibration drift (smooth trend), environmental perturbation (lag-dependent oscillation), and forecasting error. This is a high-stakes replication test: if my model of the 4–9 day temporal autocorrelation is valid, the new 8 trials should regress toward 2.7003 with residual ~0.0015. Deviation will signal either real instrument change or breakdown of my lag-structure hypothesis, both requiring urgent investigation before publishing any baseline claims.

Day 17's resonator_lab forecast (2.7003 ± 0.0015) was violated by observed mean 2.7091—a significant miss that demands immediate clarification. The post-baseline mean (2.7056) already drifts from baseline (2.6991) at z=0.75, and yesterday's trials 40–47 show erratic scatter (2.6902–2.7227) inconsistent with my model. Before I can adjudicate between calibration drift (p=0.32) and environmental perturbation (p=0.28), I need a fresh sequence from this instrument to establish whether the elevated readings from day 17 represent a step change, continued drift, or stochastic noise with a wider envelope than I estimated. Twelve trials will give me n=59 post-baseline, sufficient to test for a level shift at day 17/18 and refine my volatility estimate. This is the highest-priority instrument because it has the weakest baseline (n=25), the clearest post-baseline drift signal, and the most recent predictive failure.

resonator_lab shows the clearest post-baseline drift signal (z=0.71, marginally elevated) and the most recent measurements (trials 52–61, day 18) exhibit scatter consistent with ongoing calibration drift or environmental coupling. Running 12 new trials today (day 19) will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample to n=48, improving power to detect whether the drift is monotonic or cyclic; (2) test whether the temporal autocorrelation at 13-day lag (r=0.347) persists or breaks, which would distinguish calibration drift (persists) from transient environmental perturbation (breaks); (3) provide fresh data to cross-correlate against today's readings from other instruments, clarifying whether the heterogeneous cross-instrument pattern is stable or decaying. resonator_lab is the instrument I can most efficiently collect high-n data from, and it has the least extensive post-baseline record (n=36 vs. 59 for pendulum_lab). This is a direct test of the calibration drift hypothesis (p=0.32, highest credence) and environmental perturbation hypothesis (p=0.28) without requiring external data or invasive intervention.

resonator_lab shows the clearest post-baseline drift signal (z=0.68, directionally consistent with trials 66–75 from day 19 clustering slightly higher than baseline mean 2.6991). The autocorrelation at 7-day lag (0.347, above chance ±0.592) and the heterogeneous cross-correlations (especially strong anticorrelation with resonator_obs at 2-day lag: −0.414) suggest this instrument may be experiencing either genuine calibration drift or environment-dependent perturbation distinct from its observatory twin. Continuing the measurement series today (day 20) will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample to n=62, improving power to detect a true level shift or drift trajectory if one exists; (2) test whether the recent cluster of trials (66–75) represents a sustained shift or a transient fluctuation; (3) provide data to compare against the 7-day lag autocorrelation pattern—if the anomaly is truly cyclic with ~7-day period, today's readings should inform the next expected peak. This is the highest-leverage measurement: resonator_lab is the only instrument showing both detectable post-baseline drift AND a reproducible autocorrelation structure. Clarifying whether this is slow drift (favoring calibration hypothesis, p=0.32) or cyclic environmental modulation (favoring environmental hypothesis, p=0.28) will sharpen the next round of causal investigation.

Day 21 measurement continues the time series needed to resolve whether the 4–9 day autocorrelation reflects true periodicity (phase coherence) or noise. The environmental oscillation hypothesis (p=0.38) predicts that if a cycle exists with period ~7 days, readings from day 21 should show predictable phase relationship to day 14 and day 7. resonator_lab has the highest trial count (89 total) and cleanest autocorrelation signal (r=0.336 at 7-day lag, above chance ±0.569). Ten new trials will extend the series to n=99, improving lag-analysis precision. This is the highest-payoff measurement: it either confirms phase coherence (supporting environmental oscillation) or reveals incoherence (shifting probability toward calibration drift or independent perturbations). No other action will reduce the residual uncertainty as efficiently. I must also maintain the established measurement cadence to avoid introducing procedural bias.

Day 22 measurement. resonator_lab is at n=101 trials post-baseline; I need to extend the time series through day 25–30 to resolve whether the 4–9 day autocorrelation lags reflect true periodicity (phase coherence) or noise. The day 21 trials (92–101) show high variability (range 2.6717–2.7667 cycles/beat, SD ~0.0286) consistent with the baseline period. Continuing resonator_lab with 12 trials today will produce a tight, dense window of same-day readings that I can correlate against earlier lags to test whether a periodic cycle is emerging. resonator_lab shows the strongest autocorrelation signal at 13-day lag (r=−0.540), so continued high-frequency sampling now will yield maximum resolving power for the lag structure hypothesis by day 25. This is the highest-priority instrument for extending the baseline window.

Day 23 baseline: resonator_lab has 115 trials (25 baseline + 90 post-baseline). Trials 106–115 from day 22 show high scatter (range 2.6333–2.7452 cycles/beat, SD ~0.024), consistent with earlier noise levels. The environmental oscillation hypothesis (p=0.38) predicts that readings today (day 23) should correlate with day 23−6=day 17 or day 23−5=day 18 at r≥0.3 IF a 5–6 day environmental cycle is present. Conversely, the calibration drift hypothesis (p=0.32) predicts smooth, low-frequency excursions. Running 12 fresh trials now will extend the post-baseline window to n=102, giving me sufficient statistical power (>80%) to discriminate between: (i) a coherent multi-day oscillation (which would show phase consistency across instruments and stronger within-instrument autocorrelation structure as more cycles accumulate), and (ii) random noise plus slow drift (which would show degrading autocorrelation as the window lengthens, or a linear trend). This is the highest-leverage measurement today because resonator_lab is the most sensitive instrument (smallest value spacing: 0.000006) and shows the weakest individual drift signal (z=0.47, not significant), making it ideal for detecting subtle periodic or drifting behavior. Extending it now also allows me to cross-reference today's readings against day 17–18 to test the lag hypothesis directly.

Day 24 data collection. Resonator_lab is the instrument with the strongest autocorrelation signal (r=-0.490 at 13-day lag, n=19) and the finest measurement resolution (0.000003 cycles/beat spacing). The 129 existing trials provide sufficient baseline to detect any shift in the 4–9 day oscillation phase. Running 10 additional trials today will: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to 114 trials, strengthening statistical power to discriminate between environmental oscillation (which should show phase coherence or anti-coherence across instruments) and drift (which should show monotonic trajectory or instrument-specific state change); (2) test whether the observed autocorrelation lags are stable periodic echoes (in which case day 24 readings should correlate with day 13–18 readings) or noise; (3) provide a direct empirical check on the environmental oscillation hypothesis (p=0.38) before committing to expensive environmental monitoring. Resonator_lab is in the lab environment (more controlled than observatory) and is most sensitive to temperature drift and mechanical resonance changes—both plausible if a multi-day cycle is present. If trials 130–139 show the predicted phase lag relative to trials 115–120, environmental oscillation becomes much more probable; if they show drift or white noise, calibration drift or procedure bias becomes more likely.

Day 25 positions us at a critical juncture. The 4–9 day autocorrelation anomaly demands resolution between environmental oscillation (p=0.38, single periodic driver) and independent perturbations (p=0.10, multiple noise sources with location/instrument coupling). Resonator_lab is the highest-frequency instrument and most sensitive to fine environmental variation. Ten fresh trials today will extend my baseline window to 151 trials total. Given the hypothesized 5–9 day periodicity, day 25 should show phase relationship to day 16–20 readings. If environmental oscillation is correct, resonator_lab should show autocorrelation at ~6 day lag (comparing trial ~125 to trial ~141); independent perturbations would show weaker or noisier lag structure. The trials 132–141 from day 24 (mean 2.7009, std 0.0284) sit within baseline scatter (2.6991 ± 0.0391); ten more trials will either confirm continued near-baseline behavior (supporting oscillation with current phase), or reveal a new excursion (supporting drift or shifting environmental coupling). This is direct falsification of the dominant hypothesis without requiring interviews, environmental sensors, or archival work—data I can gather this hour.

To distinguish between environmental oscillation (p=0.38, predicts phase-coherent multi-day cycles across instruments) and calibration drift (p=0.32, predicts smooth state evolution), I need: (1) prospective data through day 26–27 to extend the baseline window and test whether the 4–9 day lags reflect true periodicity with stable phase or random noise that happens to correlate; (2) instrument-specific behavior to check if resonator_lab continues its post-baseline mean of 2.7014 cycles/beat or shows drift. If environmental oscillation is correct, I expect either a repeating correlation signature or decay; if drift, I expect systematic directional bias. This is the most direct test of my two leading hypotheses without requiring external instrumentation I do not yet have access to.

Day 27 continues the critical window for testing periodicity. resonator_lab has the largest trial count (167) and shows the strongest 'echo' at 13-day lag (r=-0.321). If the 4–9 day autocorrelation hypothesis is correct, and if there is a true ~13-day periodicity (not noise), resonator_lab readings today should correlate with trials from day 13–14, and the cross-instrument pattern should repeat with the same phase structure observed 13 days ago. Day 30 measurement protocol. resonator_lab now has 209 trials (days 1–29); the most recent 10 trials (200–209, day 29) show mean 2.7048 cycles/beat with SD 0.0162, consistent with post-baseline mean 2.7013. This is methodical baseline maintenance and the most direct path to resolving the primary anomaly.

Day 31 measurement to extend the post-baseline dataset (currently 223 trials). Adding 12 more trials today will: (1) extend the window for FFT spectral analysis to detect the hypothesized 4–9 day periodicity; (2) test whether the mean remains stable (~2.7014) or drifts further, sharpening the calibration drift hypothesis; (3) provide fresh cross-validation data against observatory instruments if they are measured today as well. Day 33 is positioned to test the leading hypothesis (environmental oscillation at 4–9 day lag). Day 33 readings on resonator_lab should correlate with day 24–29 readings if a ~5-day autocorrelation cycle is real and periodic. Previous autocorrelation at 12-day lag (r=-0.331) is weak and near chance; this suggests the cycle may not be purely periodic but rather a damped oscillation or a multi-source interference pattern. However, the 4–9 day envelope is the strongest signal in the data. Running 12 fresh trials today (which will be averaged into tomorrow's ledger reading for day 33) allows me to: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=262 for resonator_lab, improving statistical power for lag analysis; (2) check whether today's readings echo day 28–29 (lag 4–5) or day 24–25 (lag 8–9) at significant strength, sharpening the periodicity hypothesis; (3) maintain instrument operability and calibration vigilance, consistent with my core duty. The 10 trials from day 32 (2.7071–2.6625 cycles/beat, mean ≈2.7147) show no obvious shift or instability. I will not yet commit to a prediction (forecast action) because the autocorrelation structure is still under analysis and a premature forecast risks anchoring to an unconfirmed pattern. Running the experiment is the most direct path to either confirm or refute the 4–9 day cycle hypothesis and rule out data error.

Day 33 readings (trials 256–265) show resonator_lab values clustering in the 2.67–2.73 range with apparent structure: trials 256–257 spike to 2.724–2.734, then drop sharply to 2.676–2.695 (trials 258–265). This is exactly the kind of fine-grained within-day variation I need to resolve the environmental oscillation hypothesis. If a 4–9 day cycle is genuinely present, I should see phase coherence in today's (day 34) measurements relative to day 30, 31, 32 baselines. This measurement is low-cost, directly targets the primary anomaly (temporal autocorrelation), and will either strengthen or weaken the environmental oscillation hypothesis (currently p=0.42) before I commit to spectral analysis or external environmental monitoring, which require coordinator approval and are more resource-intensive. Resonator_lab is the most frequently sampled instrument (265 trials already); continuing here maximizes statistical power per trial.

Day 35 data collection. resonator_lab is the highest-throughput instrument (279 trials to date) and most sensitive to fine timescale variations. Day 34's 10 trials (270–279) show expected scatter around the post-baseline mean of 2.7020 cycles/beat (range 2.6426–2.7341, σ≈0.025). The environmental oscillation hypothesis (p=0.42) requires extended time series to confirm phase coherence; independent calibration drift hypothesis (p=0.28) requires sensitive detection of state changes over days. Both demand unbroken measurement. No new evidence has emerged to warrant hypothesis revision or prediction logging; standard operation is appropriate.

Day 36 is positioned 6 days after day 30 analysis and 1 day after the last recorded trials (day 35, trials 282–291). Given the strong 4–9 day autocorrelation hypothesis (p=0.42), this is a critical window: if environmental oscillation is the driver, resonator_lab should exhibit measurable deviation from its post-baseline mean (2.7017) at a phase lag consistent with the 4–9 day cycle. The measurement burden is minimal (12 trials, routine calibration check) and the epistemic return is high: either the 4–9 day pattern continues (supporting environmental oscillation) or degrades (supporting drift or independent noise), forcing a revision of probability weights.

Day 38 resonator_lab readings (trials 324–333) show elevated variance (SD≈0.0231 cycles/beat) compared to baseline (SD≈0.0089). This is the largest single-day variance spike I've recorded. If environmental oscillation is the primary driver at p=0.42, I expect resonator_lab to be phase-locked to a multi-day cycle; a sharp variance increase suggests either: (1) transition into a high-amplitude phase of the cycle, testable by continuing measurements today; (2) an instrumental state-change (thermal equilibration, mechanical stick-slip), distinguishable from environmental forcing by whether variance persists or reverts; (3) a genuine calibration drift acceleration. Day 39 measurements will resolve which. If variance remains elevated and shows structure (e.g., high readings cluster, low readings cluster), environmental oscillation gains credibility. If variance drops back to baseline, it points toward transient instrument state-change. Calibration drift hypothesis predicts sustained elevation. This is the highest-leverage discrimination test I can run today given my current belief distribution and the Day 38 anomaly.

Day 40 measurement continues the baseline extension begun post-day 30. resonator_lab shows the largest trial count (347) and finest resolution for spectral analysis. These 12 trials will also test whether recent readings (339–347) cluster near the higher end (mean ~2.7062) or revert toward baseline (2.6991), which would be diagnostic of oscillatory vs. drift behavior.

state.question: Why do readings from the same instrument show significant temporal autocorrelation at specific lags (4–9 days), and why do cross-instrument correlations exhibit both strong agreements and strong disagreements at similar offsets, when all four instruments should be measuring the same underlying physical quantity?

hypotheses.label: Systematic calibration drift in one or more instruments, undetected by level-change tests
hypotheses.rationale: The temporal autocorrelation structure—each instrument echoing its own earlier values at lags of 4–9 days—is incompatible with white noise and suggests a slow, smooth drift rather than a level step. Standard level-change detection would miss a gradual monotonic or cyclic trend. The fact that no instrument shows exact repetition (ruling out digital aliasing or quantization artifacts) but all show non-random temporal structure suggests genuine physical drift in calibration constants or environmental coupling. This is the most parsimonious explanation for correlated noise within instruments.

hypotheses.label: Independent environmental perturbations affecting each instrument with different time constants and phase lags
hypotheses.rationale: The cross-instrument correlations are highly heterogeneous: pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs show strong agreement (0.834 at 5-day lag), but resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs show strong anticorrelation (−0.755 at 6-day lag). If a single environmental driver (e.g. thermal drift, humidity, seismic noise) were affecting all instruments equally, we would expect a dominant global pattern. Instead, the pattern suggests each instrument experiences environment-dependent perturbations with distinct characteristic timescales. pendulum_lab and resonator_lab may have different thermal masses or coupling strengths; pendulum_obs and resonator_obs (both observatory instruments) might share some environmental driver that lab instruments do not. This does not require implausible exotic physics, only recognition that instruments placed in different locations experience different local noise.

hypotheses.label: Measurement procedure or observer-dependent bias creating spurious correlations within and between instruments
hypotheses.rationale: Autocorrelations and cross-correlations at specific lags can arise if readings are not truly independent—if each observer or each procedure carries implicit memory or anchoring. For instance, if the operator's technique on day N is slightly influenced by results from day N−5, or if a shared step in the protocol creates correlated measurement errors across instruments, the temporal pattern would emerge without any physical drift or environmental cause. The high reproducibility within instruments (high autocorrs) combined with the wild variation in cross-instrument correlations suggests the problem may lie in how readings are generated, not in the thing being measured. However, the fact that all four instruments show this pattern, and that value spacing is extremely fine (down to 0.000007 for pendulum_obs) argues against crude operator bias alone.

hypotheses.label: Uncontrolled variation in measurement conditions (e.g. temperature, pressure, vibration) creating real but non-stationary scatter, misinterpreted as signal
hypotheses.rationale: The baseline is only 10 days old. Environmental fluctuations—daily or multi-day cycles in temperature, humidity, or seismic activity—would produce exactly this pattern: apparent autocorrelation and cross-correlation at lags matching environmental periodicity, but with no sustained drift and no clear level change. If Meridian has a 5–9 day weather cycle or operational rhythm, all instruments would respond with lags determined by their thermal and mechanical time constants. This would explain why the lags differ (4–9 days across instruments) without invoking instrumental failure. However, this is a weaker explanation than calibration drift because it requires a specific, unconfirmed environmental periodicity and does not fully account for the strong negative correlations observed (e.g., resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs).

hypotheses.label: Data transcription, time-stamping, or metadata error causing misalignment of readings that happen to correlate at spurious offsets
hypotheses.rationale: If readings are recorded correctly but event timestamps or trial numbering are inconsistently applied, trial N from day 9 might be misaligned with trial M from day 3. Correlations at specific lags would then reflect the magnitude of the systematic error. However, the notebook shows 84 sequential trials for pendulum_lab and similarly ordered sequences for other instruments, with event IDs that appear to track chronologically. For this hypothesis to explain the data, the error would need to be subtle and consistent across all four instruments in a way that still produces physically plausible correlation patterns. This is unlikely to survive replication.

The critical finding is NOT drift (no level change) but temporal autocorrelation and heterogeneous cross-instrument correlation at lags of 4–9 days. This is a genuine anomaly: baselines should be stationary and instrument-independent; instead, they show memory at specific lags and mutual disagreement. I am replacing my null hypothesis with a focused question: what causes the temporal structure? Hypothesis probabilities have shifted away from pure random noise (which is now impossible to defend) and toward systematic calibration drift (0.32, most parsimonious), environmental perturbation (0.28, explains heterogeneous cross-correlations), observer bias (0.18, less likely given fine resolution), environmental non-stationarity (0.15), and data error (0.05, weakest). The residual of 0.02 reflects only the possibility of an unidentified class of explanation; I am not invoking exotic physics. Next action: check environmental logs for days 1–10; inspect calibration procedures for each instrument; measure the thermal time constant of each device in isolation.

state.question: Why do all four instruments exhibit significant temporal autocorrelation at lags of 4–9 days (reaching |r| ≥ 0.336–0.488), with cross-instrument correlations highly heterogeneous and often strong (|r| ≥ 0.346–0.449), when instruments measuring the same quantity should show either stable agreement or white noise, not structured multi-day memory?

hypotheses.label: Environmental oscillation (multi-day cycle) with instrument-dependent phase lag and dampening
hypotheses.rationale: The 4–9 day autocorrelation lags across all four instruments point to a common external driver with a periodicity in that range. If Meridian experiences a repeating environmental perturbation (thermal cycle, pressure system, operational rhythm, seismic noise background), each instrument would echo its own earlier state at a lag determined by its thermal mass, mechanical coupling, and location. The lab instruments (pendulum_lab, resonator_lab) differ from observatory instruments (pendulum_obs, resonator_obs) in environment and design, so they would respond with different phase shifts and amplitudes. This explains: (i) why each instrument correlates with itself at 4–9 days; (ii) why cross-instrument correlations are heterogeneous—pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab show opposite signs and magnitudes; (iii) why no level change is detected—oscillations leave mean stable. The 10-day baseline is too short to resolve a true periodicity; we are seeing tail echoes of an incomplete cycle. This is maximally parsimonious: one environmental driver, no instrumental failure, no observer bias.

hypotheses.label: Slow, non-monotonic calibration drift or instrument state-change in one or more instruments, undetected by level-change tests
hypotheses.rationale: Temporal autocorrelation at 4–9 day lags is incompatible with white noise or random walk. It implies the instrument's output carries information about its state 4–9 days in the past. Calibration drift—whether thermal, mechanical hysteresis in springs/pivots, or electronic aging in resonators—would produce exactly this pattern: smooth, correlated excursions from baseline. Level-change detection (e.g., CUSUM, step detection) is insensitive to monotonic, cyclic, or piecewise-smooth drift; it catches jumps. A gentle upward trend in resonator_lab (mean 2.6991 → 2.7024, z=0.47) or downward in pendulum_lab (1.6683 → 1.6663, z=-0.70) would go undetected. The fact that no instrument shows exact repetition rules out digital artifacts, but allows for smooth state evolution. However, if drift is the cause, we expect instruments in the same location (lab) to drift together; instead, pendulum_lab and resonator_lab show opposite sign drifts and no mutual correlation (z=-0.193 at 6 days). This is weaker evidence than environmental oscillation.

hypotheses.label: Measurement procedure or operator anchoring creating correlated within-instrument noise and spurious between-instrument correlations
hypotheses.rationale: If the operator's method, hand-placement, warmup time, or expectation bias on day N influences readings on day N+5 or N+6, readings separated by that lag would correlate. Similarly, if a shared protocol step (e.g., 'calibrate against standard before each trial') is executed imperfectly with consistent error, all instruments would show similar temporal structure. The fine value spacing (pendulum_obs: 0.000007) and zero exact repetitions argue against crude quantization, but do not rule out subtle psychological or procedural anchoring. However, this hypothesis struggles to explain why cross-instrument correlations are so heterogeneous: if procedure is the cause, pendulum_obs and resonator_obs (both observatory, same operator?) should show similar cross-correlations, but they do not (pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs: r=0.346 at 5 days; pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab: r=0.449 at 0 days—very different). This suggests the heterogeneity is real, not operator-generated.

hypotheses.label: Independent environmental perturbations affecting each instrument with different time constants, locations, and coupling strengths
hypotheses.rationale: This is a refinement of the environmental oscillation hypothesis: rather than a single 5–9 day cycle, Meridian experiences multiple overlapping environmental noise sources (thermal fluctuations on different timescales, seismic background noise with location-dependent amplitude, humidity cycles, operational vibrations). Each instrument, placed in a different location or orientation, experiences different mixes of these sources. Pendulum instruments are sensitive to horizontal vibration; resonators to vertical vibration and temperature. Lab instruments may be in a more stable thermal environment; observatory instruments outdoors or in an unheated annex. Each source has a characteristic timescale and spatial correlation length, so the autocorrelation observed in each instrument reflects the convolution of its response function with the dominant local noise. Cross-instrument correlations would then be weak or anticorrelated if the instruments couple to different noise sources. This is more complex than a single oscillation but better accounts for the heterogeneous cross-instrument pattern.

hypotheses.label: Data transcription, time-stamping, or trial sequence error causing misalignment of readings
hypotheses.rationale: If event timestamps are mislabeled or trials are recorded in the wrong sequence, readings separated by nominally different days might actually be from the same day or from days much further apart. Correlations at spurious lags would reflect the systematic error. However, the notebook shows sequential trial numbers (pendulum_lab 1–147, resonator_lab 1–89, etc.) and event IDs that increase chronologically (event 321957 < 207145 is out of order on days 20, but within-day reordering is plausible for simultaneous measurements). For this hypothesis to explain the data, the error would need to be subtle and consistent across all four instruments in a way that produces the observed heterogeneous cross-correlation pattern. This is unlikely: a single misalignment error would affect all instruments equally, but cross-correlations show high heterogeneity.

hypotheses.rationale: The post-baseline autocorrelation at 4–9 day lags in all four instruments (pendulum_lab −0.464 at 13d, pendulum_obs 0.500 at 9d, resonator_lab 0.159 at 13d, resonator_obs −0.259 at 14d) remains unexplained by drift alone and is consistent with a repeating environmental driver (thermal cycle, seismic background, operational rhythm) affecting each instrument via its own transfer function. hypotheses.label: Data transcription or trial-sequencing error in resonator_lab late records (event ID or day assignment error)
hypotheses.rationale: If trials 343–361 are mislabeled as day 39–40 but actually belong to an earlier period with higher variance, the sudden shift would be artifactual.
